fullText:
The mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birding

On a brilliantly bright afternoon in his gallery and studio in Bolinas, a small town on the northern California coast, Keith Hansen was putting the finishing touches on a watercolor of an almost improbably flamboyant painted bunting.

With an ultra-fine sable brush, he made a few intricate additions to the cobalt blue plumage on the bunting’s head, and, satisfied with his work, slipped the watercolor into a stout binder that every few days welcomes a new addition.

“That was number 420,” he said. Or to put it another way, just 584 to go.

Hansen, a renowned ornithological illustrator and author, has a monumental task – a hand-painted compendium of every one of the roughly 1,000 bird species ever recorded from the US and Canada, including those found in waters up to 200 miles from shore, Hawaiian birds not included. When finished, it will complete the visual backbone of an app called Flock, whose mission, compared with that of most apps, is quietly subversive.

For rather than seeking to monopolize and monetize its users’ attention, it deftly employs elements of computer gaming and social networking to draw people outward, into the world of birding, with the broader aim of cultivating a community of conservationists.

Flock was conceived and created by two of Hansen’s friends, Adam Donkin and Bob Stevenson. Both have impressive tech industry CVs. Donkin, 52, who lives not far from Hansen in Marin county’s San Geronimo valley, worked for many years as a product and user experience designer. As a lead product designer at Amazon, he led the charge on design for several models of the Kindle e-reader.

Stevenson, a 58-year-old Scotsman, lives in St Helena in the Napa valley. He founded his first company in Edinburgh at 18, and at 24, moved to California to work as an art director for Richard Branson’s Virgin Games, embarking on a decades-long career as an art or design director, or as a producer, for more than 50 video games.

Despite their disparate disciplines, the three friends are united by a shared passion for birds and birding.

Hansen fell in love with the avian world in sixth grade, when, on a walk in the Maryland woods, his brother, Rob, drew his attention to a cedar waxwing. “It’s just an exquisite bird,” Hansen recalled. He began illustrating birds during his senior year of high school, and in 1986 – after a decade and a half observing and studying birds on numerous expeditions – he settled in Bolinas, opening his gallery there in 1991.

Donkin grew up on the San Francisco peninsula and began birding at the age of four under the wing of his father’s friend Rich Stallcup, an esteemed ornithologist and birder, and a founder of the Point Reyes Bird Observatory. “He was like a nature wizard,” said Donkin. “Birds and animals would appear when you were in the field with him. He knew every bird by call and by sight.”

Donkin moved to Marin in 2012. “When I moved to Marin,” he said, “Rich introduced me to the thriving birding community here, including Keith.”

That same year, Stevenson was looking for a designer for his new company. “One of our investors recommended that we chat with this designer, Adam,” said Stevenson. “It was meant to be a quick call, but we ended up talking for over an hour. We became friends on the first call.”

In 2016, Donkin visited Stevenson at his home in the southern Marin town of Tiburon, overlooking Richardson Bay, a major habitat for migrating waterbirds. “One day Adam came round to the house,” Stevenson recalled. “I didn’t know that he was an avid birder. He turned up and said, ‘Hey, dude, you’ve got to bird! Do you have binoculars?’”

Stevenson, who had recently stepped away from his company to focus on his family, fell hard and fast for birding. He bought binoculars, scopes and cameras, began birding from his deck, and, as an outlet for his avian photography, opened his own gallery in Tiburon.

He was also struck by the ways in which birding resembled multi-player gaming, in that it involved learning new skills, a mastery curve, collecting (by way of so-called yard lists and life lists – tabulations of the bird species sighted in one’s yard, or over a lifetime), an awareness of how one is progressing relative to others, and a community which, while competitive, helps its members learn more quickly. He also recognized, at the age of 48, what he had given up by trading the beauty of the natural world for computer screens. “It was such a revelation, because going back to nature at that age, you realize what you’ve been missing.”

Shortly after, he and Donkin began discussing the idea of building an app around birding. For Donkin, his friend’s newfound passion was a catalyst. “I had the experience with Bob of turning someone on to it, and seeing what a huge impact it had on him.”

For Stevenson, the spark was a conversation with Robert Snow, the president of the Fresno Audubon Society, who said the organization was concerned about its ability to bring future generations into birding, as this was critical to perpetuating its mission of protecting birds and their habitats.

To Donkin, the path from birding to conservation is a natural progression. “Birding creates an infinite well of curiosity,” he said. “You start to notice things and think, ‘Well, how can I help?’ You might start with providing water, providing food, providing shelter. By restoring habitat in your area, you can have an impact. It could be your yard, a park in your neighborhood, sometimes ranch land, sometimes public land.”

Initially Stevenson and Donkin thought they might develop an app in partnership with Audubon, or with the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in Ithaca, New York, where they had given a presentation on the parallels between birding and gaming, with an eye towards how aspects of game design could be employed to increase engagement with the Cornell Lab’s Merlin app, which identifies birds based on their songs and calls, or images.

They ultimately decided to strike out on their own and, in 2017, set to work on Flock. Having worked on projects backed by publishers and by investors in Silicon Valley, Stevenson said they decided to fund it themselves “so we would not be bound by anyone’s rules”. They also set out to break the addictive conventions of app design. “The games industry is so comfortable making experiences that are so engaging that you can’t look away,” said Donkin, “and we were very aware of the negative aspects of social media.”

“We didn’t want to make something that got you addicted to the dopamine hit of getting a like, or followers,” Donkin continued. “We wanted to make something that was a companion to the experience of birding. In an attention-based economy, we’re going to use that same system, but we’re going to flip it. We’re not trying to get your attention on the app, we’re trying to get your attention away from your phone so that you can then turn your attention outward.”

The result is an app whose interface is refreshingly spare and minimalistic, with a tab where users can search for birds or for other users; another for recording sightings, made, perhaps with the aid of the Merlin app or an old-fashioned field guide; a leaderboard which ranks users according to the number of unique species they saw in the current month; and a community tab where users can upload photos, message one another, and congratulate other users on their sightings.

As with every detail of the app, even the way in which users cheer one another on was carefully considered. Instead of a “like” button, there is a “high-five” button. “We put ‘high five’ rather than ‘like’,” Stevenson explained, “because kids were using it, and we wanted it to be, ‘Nice job on seeing that bird!’ rather than, ‘I like you.’ We didn’t want kids to collect likes.”

They enlisted their longtime friend Hansen, whose artistic sensitivity brought a unique beauty to the app. While Stevenson coded, Donkin scanned and processed new batches of illustrations as Hansen completed them, following an algorithm that sorted the bird species in order from the most- to the least-commonly seen. Given that it can take Hansen up to four days to complete an illustration, this prioritized the birds Flock users are more likely to encounter: an American robin or a northern cardinal, for instance, rather than a Steller’s sea eagle, a huge Siberian raptor, one of which, acting on some unknown impulse in 2020, flew from northern Asia to Alaska and then Texas, before settling on the coast of Maine.

In early 2025, they released Flock on Apple’s app store. By April of that year, Flock had about 100 users. Today, although Donkin and Stevenson have not yet done anything in the way of marketing, it has on the order of 1,000. Among the recent enhancements they enjoy are uncannily realistic animations that bring Hansen’s illustrations to life. The short animations – which Stevenson created with AI, with Hansen’s guidance – give a sense of the way each particular bird moves. The formerly static white-crowned sparrow now darts its head this way and that in a most sparrow-like fashion, peering inquisitively at its viewer; the great blue heron, meanwhile, tiptoes along a sandy bank, and pausing, stealthily lowers its bill to the water’s surface, preparing to strike.

Among Flock’s growing flock is Amy Tan, the bestselling writer whose most recent work, The Backyard Bird Chronicles, grew from a series of pencil sketches, color portraits and journal notes she collected on her avian neighbors during the pandemic. A friend of Hansen’s for 10 years, and more recently of Stevenson’s, Tan logged her first sightings in the app late last summer. In an email, Tan wrote that Flock was “hands down the most beautiful bird app and the easiest one to track and share sightings of my backyard birds. With each bird I add to my daily list, I feel rewarded when its illustration suddenly comes to life. All my friends are blown away and become instant fans.”

This reporter, meanwhile, who entered his first sighting – a western gull – in Flock last spring, has found himself growing ever more attuned to the sights, sounds and habits of his feathered compatriots in San Francisco, and has recently begun shopping for a hummingbird feeder.

title: Pritchard eyes world title defence after Euro win
description: The 34-year-old from Mumbles, near Swansea will head to Amsterdam having overcome a freak pre-Europeans injury to retain his title in Italy.
fullText:
Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard hopes his successful European title defence can be the springboard to retaining his world title later this month.

The 34-year-old will head to Amsterdam having overcome a freak pre-event injury to beat Italian Giacomo Perini in the PR1 men's single sculls at the European Rowing Championships in Varese, Italy last weekend.

"When I landed in Italy, there was a malfunction on the hoist that got me on to the coach and the cable snapped, so it dropped me from the top of the hoist to the bottom, which obviously causes a bit of an injury, which I was managing throughout the championships," Pritchard told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Pritchard, from Mumbles, Swansea, added: "I actually thought I may not have come out on top given the injury that I was coping with, but I'm glad I did. It was a great race though.

"It's probably one of the best races we've had in in a couple of years because it was neck and neck until the last 250m."

Pritchard named BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year 2025

Pritchard, the BBC Cymru Wales Sports Personality of the Year for 2025, and his Great Britain team-mates have stayed at Varese to complete their preparations for the World Rowing Championships, that take place from 24-30 August at Amsterdam's Bosbaan venue.

"I always feel that this this camp is where we get the most speed," said Pritchard.

"We do a load of speed work in this last block now for the world championships, so I'm hoping that that'll set me in good stead for the future.

"I have just seen my competitor Erik Horrie from Australia training this morning, and he looks really fast as well. So hopefully we can get a good race but it's an outdoor sport - anything could happen.

"But it's going to be nice to be out on the Bosbaan in Amsterdam because the Welsh men's hockey team and ladies' team have got their World champs as well, so I'm going to hopefully get across and watch some of their games too."

Pritchard is one of Para-rowing's dominant forces. Since winning gold at the 2024 Paralympics he has set multiple world records in his event and added the 2025 European and world crowns to his tally.

He says he went to Italy with added desire to succeed after his Swansea coach Andrew Williams lost his father.

"It was a big one and an emotional one, but gave you the actual motivation when the going got tough in the race, that's for sure," he said.

However, Pritchard was comfortable facing and beating Perini on his home waters, saying: "I think it's more my home water than his.

"You know, we're in his home country, but as a team, we come here twice a year to train and spend two weeks of time here, so I've been coming here now for nine years.

"It feels like a home to me, and the club members know me and all that kind of stuff, so I feel that actually I had a good share of the support in the stands."

title: 'Having skill is one thing': Shikhar Dhawan drops big verdict on Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

fullText:
Former India opener Shikhar Dhawan has praised teenage batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, saying the youngster's fearless batting and ability to perform at such a young age make him special.

Speaking to news agency ANI, Dhawan said it is a big achievement for a 15-year-old to reach the international level and deliver consistent performances. He also pointed to Sooryavanshi's IPL displays, saying the teenager's confidence in hitting boundaries stands out.

Dhawan said talent alone is not enough, and added that having the courage and mindset to play attacking cricket at such a young age is what sets Sooryavanshi apart. He also backed the youngster to continue doing well in the years ahead.

"He is batting very superbly. And it's a very big thing that at the age of 15 or 16, reaching the international level first is a big thing in itself. Even when he was playing in the IPL. But the way he hits fours and sixes, that's a wonderful thing. Having skill is one thing, but having the heart for it, and that too at 15, is a very big thing. And I'm sure that his present is also very good and his future will also be very good," Dhawan said.

Sooryavanshi, 15, recently enjoyed a successful T20I series against Zimbabwe, scoring 151 runs in three matches to win his maiden Player of the Series award as India completed a 3-0 clean sweep.

Earlier, during the T20I series against England, Sooryavanshi became the youngest player to make his international debut for India.

His India debut came after a successful IPL 2026 season with Rajasthan Royals. He scored 776 runs at a strike rate of 237.30, including one century and five fifties. He finished as the tournament's highest run-scorer and hit a record 72 sixes.

Sooryavanshi also won the Orange Cap, Most Valuable Player, Emerging Player, Super Striker and Super Sixes awards after the season.

Earlier this year, he also impressed in the ICC Men's Under-19 Cricket World Cup, scoring 439 runs and winning the Player of the Tournament award.

title: Saudi Arabia turns to Muslim military heavyweights in landmark defense pact as Iran war closes in
description: Saudi Arabia has drawn two of the Muslim world’s most formidable military powers into its defense as the Iran war moves closer to the kingdom.
fullText:
Saudi Arabia has drawn two of the Muslim world's most formidable military powers into its defense as the Iran war moves closer to the kingdom.

Pakistan and Turkey signed a NATO-style mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia in Mecca on Friday, consolidating their longstanding security ties into a collective-defense alliance that stipulates an attack against any of them "shall be regarded as attack on them all."

That commitment could draw Pakistan and Turkey into a war they have carefully kept at arm's length.

The official rationale for the agreement is "to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression" and further provide "for the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three states," according to a statement released by all three countries.

More specifically, the pact gives Saudi Arabia a powerful new layer of protection beyond its longstanding security partnership with the United States amid growing regional doubts over whether Washington can still be relied upon to protect its oil-rich Gulf allies.

Turkey has the second-largest military in NATO, behind only the US, while Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim nation.

Such powerful allies strengthen Saudi deterrence and present a united Sunni-led military front against a mounting Iranian threat, though a Turkish official told CNN the agreement isn't directed against any specific actor and the Saudi foreign ministry insisted this "does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc."

Other regional countries can also join, the Turkish official added, raising the prospect of the alliance drawing in new members much like NATO.

The statement ⁠did not give specifics on the commitments each had accepted, and it is unclear how far the agreement would bind the three countries to any particular military action in each other's defence.

The pact also comes as Israel expands its military reach across the region and Riyadh's relations with the neighboring United Arab Emirates fray.

Pakistan and Turkey each share a border with Iran and both have strong reasons to prevent the conflict from spiraling. Pakistan must manage its sizeable Shiite population and its sensitive relationship with Tehran, while Turkey and Iran share concerns over Kurdish separatism despite competing elsewhere in the region.

Tehran repeatedly struck targets in Saudi Arabia during the war, including civilian infrastructure, energy facilities and US interests. Direct Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia largely subsided after an April 8 ceasefire took hold, but Iran-backed groups in Yemen and Iraq continued targeting the kingdom.

title: Rashid takes six wickets as Afghanistan thrash Ireland
description: Rashid Khan takes six wickets as Afghanistan beat Ireland by 92 runs in Gary Wilson's first one-day international as head coach.
fullText:
Afghanistan 299-8 (47 overs): Zadran 84 (97); Adair 2-40

Ireland 207 all out (33.4 overs): Carmichael 62 (66); Rashid 6-34

Rashid Khan took six wickets as Afghanistan beat Ireland by 92 runs in Gary Wilson's first one-day international as head coach.

After Wednesday's opener if the five-game series was washed out without a ball bowled, a wet outfield at Bready led to a 90-minute delay and a reduction of three overs per side.

Afghanistan quickly took advantage of the short boundaries at the County Tyrone ground, with a succession of batters looking set even if it was only Ibrahim Zadran who went on to pass fifty.

His 84 helped Afghanistan post 299-8 ,but Ireland could only muster 207 as Wilson's reign started with defeat.

Cade Carmichael was Ireland's top scorer with 62, but Rashid stole the show with six wickets.

The tourists have won seven ODIs against Ireland in succession, a run that stretches back to 2019.

Ireland's first ODI with Afghanistan washed out

As has been the case throughout this home summer, Ireland's bowling options were limited through injuries.

Josh Little, Matt Hollard, Craig Young and Barry McCarthy were all enforced absentees, with Wilson's first selection showing four specialist bowlers including international debutant Byron McDonough.

There was plenty of interest to see how Jai Moondra, breakout star of June's T20 series victory over India, would fare in his one-day bow with the India-born 29-year-old's two wickets coming at a cost of 78 runs.

title: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual after the failed World Cup private investment plan - but it may not be that easy.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino stepped off a plane in Cali and was greeted on the runway by the president of the Colombian Football Federation.

Ramon Jesurun, a close ally of Infantino's, saw it as a chance to show his support, with the two men smiling in a photo opportunity for the federation's Instagram account.

Infantino had not travelled to Colombia for any run-of-the-mill meeting on Friday. He would attend the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Infantino was accompanied by Alejandro Dominguez, the president of South America's football governing body Conmebol, who praised both his record and the "enormously successful" 2026 World Cup, saying "we stand with Gianni".

This is the life of a Fifa president.

It involves building ties with some of the most powerful people in the world, shown by Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Before the biggest scandal to hit his tenure - the aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise plan - Infantino was an incredibly powerful figure who appeared bulletproof.

Now, after an apology and stated desire to withstand the backlash of his plan to sell a stake in the men's World Cup to private equity firms, Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual.

Uefa's threat to boycott Fifa tournaments still stands. That will be tested with the Fifa Under-20 World Cup set to kick off in Poland in 29 days.

Perhaps emboldened by the support he has received from outside Europe in recent days, Infantino is not going to stand down easily.

But what exactly is the role of the Fifa president?

A cavalcade of blacked out Mercedes, flanked by police cars, rolled into the Fifa headquarters in Rabat, Morocco, earlier this week.

Infantino had summoned a select few members of the Fifa management board to discuss his plan to sell off 21% of the commercial and ticketing business to a private equity firm.

This is how the Swiss-Italian travels - in between flights on the Qatar Airways Executive jet which has been made available to him. The plane enabled him to take up to three flights a day, watching two games, throughout the 2026 World Cup.

That type of arrival does look presidential - only more like a president of a country than a sports body.

It enables him to travel the globe, visiting Fifa's official offices like Rabat, where he was based over the past week as the Fifa Forward Enterprise controversy developed.

In his role Infantino is expected to visit the 211 member nations, to see the grassroots projects Fifa has funded.

Part of his remit is to unify football, which cannot be achieved from within the Fifa headquarters in Zurich.

It requires international travel to attend confederation meetings, and the global tournaments Fifa organises. Infantino needs to build relationships with officials and politicians.

In April, before the Fifa Congress in Vancouver, local authorities rejected a request for a level-four motorcade, usually reserved for heads of state or the Pope.

New Zealand police said they had declined a similar request during the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Alongside the cavalcade of cars and the private charter flights comes a large salary, too, three times what he first earned when elected in 2016.

Infantino, who was paid about £1.3m 10 years ago, now takes home about £4m - a base salary of £2.2m plus a confirmed variable bonus payment of £1.8m.

His predecessor Sepp Blatter was paid a £2.6m package for his final year as Fifa president.

Infantino gets a 'per diem' too to cover expenses and living costs, worth £20,500 a year on top of his salary.

As the head of the most popular sport in the world, it should be expected that there is a wage to match.

Infantino would argue that by driving record revenues and funding for member associations, he has proven he is worth the salary.

Infantino's alliance with Trump seemed to have elevated his status even further.

Many in world football felt that this began to come at the expense of his responsibilities in football.

In May 2025, Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress in Paraguay.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

There was also the Fifa Peace Prize, awarded to Trump weeks before the US invaded Venezuela to depose president Nicolas Maduro and launched air attacks on Iran.

Despite criticism, the Fifa ethics committee did not respond to complaints about Infantino's political neutrality over the prize.

At the start of the year, Infantino made a surprise appearance at the inaugural meeting of Trump's Board of Peace, set up to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza.

The International Olympic Committee, of which Infantino is an invited member, said its rules on political neutrality had not been breached.

However, many felt he had positioned himself too close to the US president.

This was heightened when USA striker Folarin Balogun escaped a ban after being sent off at the World Cup.

It was an unprecedented move by Fifa's disciplinary committee, with Trump saying he had personally called Infantino asking for the red card to be reviewed.

Infantino insisted it was a decision taken by an independent body over which no-one could have an influence.

On the final weekend of the World Cup, Trump and Infantino appeared together at Trump Tower in New York. The US president said he had called the Fifa president who "made another great decision".

Then, perhaps the culmination of Infantino's close association with Trump, came Fifa Forward Enterprise.

The private investor was to be a company linked to the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

Independent questions of Infantino's methods and decisions are rare because he does not often speak to the media.

In the past four years he has given just two news conferences, both lasting an hour and held before the start of the World Cup.

Other than that, Infantino generally appears in Fifa-produced interviews issued through their official channels.

Before the 2026 World Cup, Infantino tried to head off at the pass any queries about high ticket prices and supporters' visas.

But, at the news conference before the World Cup, his reply of "just, you know, chill, relax" about Somali referee Omar Artan, who had been denied entry to the USA at Miami Airport, sparked concern.

The Fifa statement issued on Wednesday offered some contrition. But there was a rebuke, too.

It gave Infantino the chance to bite back, saying Fifa would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process".

The allure of the role is great, underscored by the fact there have been just four permanent Fifa presidents since Stanley Rous was elected in 1961.

Outside of Europe, the record revenues achieved by Infantino have funded the football operations of many countries. That has created loyalty, and it is a vote winner.

Yet for Uefa, and a few other national associations, the rap sheet is now too long.

Fifa cannot be run as an autocratic project any longer, claim his critics - many of them within European football.

Expanding the World Cup was in Infantino's election manifesto, and an increase to 64 teams for 2030 seems highly likely if he gets a fourth term.

There was also the expanded summer Club World Cup. The trophy is engraved with a personal tribute - "Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino".

The unique allocation of the next two men's World Cups helped ensure Saudi Arabia, another close ally of Infantino, would get the 2034 event.

The draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair. Trump was front and centre, as was Infantino.

Many supporters felt the price of tickets was too high, while some who were prepared to pay for them were denied visas.

Fifa opted to use a secondary market place with uncapped prices and a 30% share on each ticket sold.

Critics said profit had become more important than the supporter experience, with the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey subpoenaing Fifa to answer questions about its ticketing practices.

Even with all these controversies, Infantino was expected to be re-elected, such was his support around the world in many member associations.

Indeed, before the World Cup 111 had already declared for him - enough to guarantee re-election.

Now that picture is uncertain amid the fallout from Fifa's failed private investment plan.

Uefa sees this moment as its chance to force him to step down.

But, as his attendance at the Colombia president's inauguration shows, that may be incredibly difficult to achieve.

title: The Anniversaries of Hiroshima and Nagasaki Have Special Meaning in a World Out of Control
description: William D. Hartung, Mari...
fullText:
As the last US-Russia nuclear arms control treaty expires, the anniversaries of Hiroshima and Nagasaki carry renewed urgency for a world edging toward a new arms race.

This August marks yet another anniversary of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, but 2026 carries a special weight—for the first time since the Cold War, the United States has no active nuclear arms control treaty with Russia, following the expiration of the New START nuclear arms reduction agreement.

Over 80 years ago, the United States dropped two atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The uranium bomb detonated over Hiroshima on August 6 destroyed an estimated 70 percent of the city’s buildings and roughly 140,000 lost their lives. Less than five days later, a plutonium bomb was dropped on the nearby city of Nagasaki, killing an additional 74,000 people, triggering radioactive rain, and driving ground temperatures above 4,000°C. In the years and decades that followed, the few survivors who lived faced immense health complications including leukemia, cancer, deformities, and other devastating health impacts from radiation—impacts those communities are still living with today.

New START itself can be traced back to the Soviet era, when the United States and Russia first launched the SALT negotiations that eventually produced the Treaty on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms: a heralded treaty, that went through multiple iterations, that many subsequently considered the last bastion constraining a renewed global nuclear arms race. That treaty expired on February 5, 2026.

In addition to the dangerous dismantling of the modest controls on nuclear escalation that had existed for decades, there has been a systematic effort to erase the devastation of the communities that have been hurt most by the development, production, and testing of nuclear weapons from our memories, and our history books. The combination of an absence of guardrails and an attempt to induce historical amnesia about the true human costs of developing and maintaining vast nuclear arsenals is a volatile mix that increases the risks that nuclear weapons might be used again, despite the lessons of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The story of nuclear weapons is more than just the story of scientists working away in secrecy at Los Alamos, or leaders wielding nuclear threats—and, in the case of the Cuban missile crisis, bringing the world to the brink of nuclear war. It is the story of devastation, disease, and death caused by the development and deployment of those weapons, even if they are never used again in warfare. The deadly consequences of nuclear development have fallen most heavily on communities of color, from the dire health consequences of mining uranium in the Congo and the American Southwest, to the generational cancers in communities downwind from nuclear tests, from the Marshall Islands to the American West; communities of color have been disproportionately affected by nuclear testing and warfare.

These consequences did not start with the bombings in Hiroshima or Nagasaki. The testing caused a reckoning that also reached into the scientific community itself, made famous by Robert Oppenheimer’s words after the Trinity test, when he said the world would not be the same, and later invoked the line “I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.” Historians still debate the racialized dimensions of why the bomb was used on Japan; questions of who counts as human, who is deemed worthy of safety, and how ideas of supremacy shape militarization remain unresolved eight decades later. That choice—its weight—also strained the diplomatic relationship between the United States and Japan, raising a question that still lingers: How does a nation set norms it did not itself follow?

The stories of the civilian victims of nuclear arms racing are increasingly at risk of being rewritten, sanitized, or erased from official histories altogether. The risks posed by the lack of arms control measures and the concerted effort to whitewash the dangers of possessing nuclear weapons, as well as the catastrophe that would come from using them, make nuclear use at some future date more likely. With no treaty framework in place, active global conflicts like the runaway wars in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine, and coordinated efforts to erase the history of nuclear dangers, we need to treat this anniversary as more than a commemoration or an expression of regret. We need to treat it as a turning point for humanity.

We need not just a moment of mourning but a call to chart a new path forward that recognizes the dreadful toll nuclear weapons have imposed, and takes fundamental steps toward reducing nuclear dangers once and for all. As the US has reached its 250th birthday, it is long past time for some truth-telling about communities harmed by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and about countries all over the world harmed by nuclear weapons.

title: Why can't the Premier League attract the world's best players?
description: Vinicius Jr chose to stay at Real Madrid, but why does the Premier League rarely attract global superstars at their peak?
fullText:
Had Vinicius Jr joined Arsenal, he would have been a rarity as a genuine global superstar moving to the Premier League at the height of his powers.

The Gunners were prepared to make the Brazil forward their primary target should he decide to leave Real Madrid, and the 26-year-old was open to the possibility.

But he has now signed a new contract at the Bernabeu until 2032.

It is another reminder of a curious contradiction.

Premier League clubs have unrivalled collective spending power and England's top flight is widely regarded as the strongest domestic competition in world football, but attracting established Ballon d'Or contenders has proved difficult.

They have little problem attracting and retaining elite centre-backs and goalkeepers but the scarcity is more obvious further forward, where the most coveted attackers and attacking midfielders still often choose elsewhere.

Since the Premier League began in 1992, only three players have won the men's Ballon d'Or while representing an English top-flight club: Liverpool's Michael Owen in 2001, Manchester United's Cristiano Ronaldo in 2008 and Manchester City's Rodri in 2024.

What England has been exceptionally good at is providing the environment in which elite talents become global stars.

Dennis Bergkamp arrived at Arsenal after a difficult spell at Inter Milan and became one of the Premier League's most influential players. Eric Cantona had already shown flashes of his talent in France and at Leeds before becoming the emblem of Manchester United's first great Premier League side.

Thierry Henry arrived in north London after an underwhelming spell at Juventus before developing into one of his generation's outstanding forwards. Ronaldo joined United as an exciting 18-year-old from Sporting, won the Ballon d'Or five years later, then signed for Real Madrid the following summer.

Erling Haaland is perhaps the clearest recent example. Already one of Europe's most coveted young forwards when Manchester City signed him from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, Haaland had yet to reach the level he has in England.

That is different from signing a player such as Vinicius after he has already won multiple Champions Leagues and established himself among the world's most recognisable footballers.

There have been exceptions, but many of the biggest names arrived after their peak.

The clearest comparison to Vinicius is Andriy Shevchenko, who joined Chelsea from AC Milan in 2006 at the age of 29. He had won the Ballon d'Or only two years earlier and finished fifth in 2005, making him one of the rare established global superstars to move to the Premier League while still close to the height of his career.

Other Ballon d'Or winners such as Ruud Gullit and George Weah also joined Chelsea, but later in their careers, while Ronaldo returned to United at 36, Zlatan Ibrahimovic arrived at 34, and Jurgen Klinsmann signed for Tottenham at 30.

During the 1980s and 1990s, Serie A was both enormously wealthy and the undisputed home of football's biggest stars.

Diego Maradona left Barcelona for Napoli. Brazil's Ronaldo moved from Barcelona to Inter at his explosive peak. Michel Platini, Marco van Basten, Lothar Matthaus and Zinedine Zidane all spent some of the finest years of their careers in Italy.

But the Premier League's financial dominance has produced a different transfer market.

English clubs spend enormous sums, but it can be distributed across deep squads or on players already proven within the competition.

Alexander Isak, Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson, Moises Caicedo, Declan Rice and Jack Grealish have all moved between Premier League clubs for more than £100m.

Others, such as Liverpool's Florian Wirtz, arrive from overseas with enormous reputations but with their best years potentially still ahead.

The model is less about importing one 'Galactico' and more about assembling 18-22 elite players capable of surviving a demanding season.

Real Madrid and Barcelona are difficult for English clubs to compete with when the world's most coveted players become available.

Jude Bellingham is a striking example. Having left Birmingham City for Borussia Dortmund to continue his development, the England midfielder moved to Real Madrid rather than back to his home country.

He remains the only player to represent England's senior men's team during the Premier League era without making an appearance in the competition.

Kylian Mbappe was linked with several clubs elsewhere before fulfilling his ambition of joining Real Madrid, while Neymar chose Barcelona over interest from Premier League teams when leaving Santos in 2013 - attracted in part by the chance to play alongside Lionel Messi.

Cristiano Ronaldo left Manchester United for Real Madrid a year after winning the Ballon d'Or, while Luis Suarez joined Barcelona months after winning the Premier League Golden Boot and PFA Players' Player of the Year with Liverpool.

And Gareth Bale and Eden Hazard swapped London for Madrid after establishing themselves among the Premier League's leading players. Bale joined Real from Tottenham in 2013 after winning the PFA Players' Player of the Year award for a second time, while Hazard made the same move from Chelsea six years later, having previously won the league's top individual honour.

Harry Kane later departed Tottenham for Bayern Munich despite sitting only 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League record of 260.

There are practical attractions to Spain - climate, lifestyle and, for many South American players, linguistic and cultural familiarity - but the appeal runs deeper.

Real Madrid and Barcelona carry a particular status as destination clubs, reinforced by their Champions League history, global reach and association with individual honours such as the Ballon d'Or.

Both have been interested in Rodri this summer.

Man City reject Barcelona's £38.5m bid for Rodri

Barcelona? Real Madrid? Man City's Rodri has a decision to make

Haaland, meanwhile, represents the counterargument. City signed him from Dortmund at 21 and he has developed into one of the world's most feared number nines.

But even his future illustrates the enduring pull of Real Madrid.

Speaking to DAZN during the 2026 World Cup, Haaland's father Alfie was asked about the prospect of the striker one day moving to the Bernabeu.

"He's happy at City, he's got a long contract… but any player wants to play for Real Madrid," he said.

That does not mean a move is imminent, but the sentiment is revealing. England has repeatedly shown it can provide the stage on which superstars are made. Persuading those already at the summit to choose the Premier League - and convincing those who reach it there to stay - remains the harder task.

title: A Research Lab for Open Source
description: Today, we're launching a world-class research lab dedicated to Open Source sustainability with a team of some of the most experienced people in the world.
fullText:
Today, we're launching a world-class research lab dedicated to Open Source sustainability with a team of some of the
most experienced people in the world.

Why? The infrastructure we all use depends on Open 
When the Open Source packages we use break, our infrastructure is at risk.

This isn't just hypothetical. It's happening already, with catastrophic global supply chain attacks such as the XZ Utils
backdoor, Log4Shell, Shai-Hulud and others.

There are efforts underway to make Open Source development more sustainable.
The Open Source Pledge has raised $7,262,189 for maintainers,
the Open Source Endowment is nearing a principal of $1m,
and excellent research is being done by
the Sovereign Tech Agency,
Alpha-Omega
and others.

But we need an organisation dedicated to answering the more general questions that Open Source sustainability depends
on. What are the most critical keystone packages? Which keystone packages appear to be maintained, but are
actually long-dead Bernies? Which dependencies are invisible to us? How can we prevent the
ever-growing issue of maintainer burnout?

One would think that one of the many well-funded Open Source foundations could tackle this research, with
a median yearly revenue of $1.6m and a mean of $11.6m. But for the most part, foundations, as a policy, do not pay
developers at all, so they cannot fund this work. This is partly a quirk of the US tax code — until the Feb 2026 launch
of the Open Source Endowment, the IRS had not recognised Open Source software as serving the public benefit, so they had
not given 501(c)(3) status to any organisation that primarily funds Open Source development.

What about for-profit companies? Some, like Chainguard and Socket are building software supply
chain analysis tools. But this work is proprietary, which doesn't sit right with our vision. The tools that allow us to
monitor our critical infrastructure are themselves critical infrastructure, so they should be publicly accessible, and
funded independently of for-profit interests.

That's why we founded the Software Stewardship Lab: a new non-profit research lab dedicated to ensuring the stability of
the Open Source ecosystem we all depend on.

We map and strengthen the Open Source ecosystem by building software, creating APIs, and writing research reports. And
our research takes into account the human side of Open Source, by investigating and caring for maintainer health.

Our team includes some of the most experienced people in the field:

We are registered as a Scottish non-profit — though our scope is global — and our values
and articles legally bind us to serving the public good and making all our work publicly accessible.
Our independent non-executive directors hold us accountable.

“If we don't secure the software supply chain, the vast majority of software will suffer.  The Software Stewardship
 Lab has a collection of world-class experts in addressing problems like this and represents perhaps the most
 ambitious effort today to solve the key problems in a fundamental manner.”

Our current research focuses are:

Moving forward, the Lab's experts will direct funding to and supervise Open Source sustainability researchers doing
critical work. We are already working with universities to teach the next generations of software supply chain experts.

And we are also working with our solicitors on achieving charity status. Charity regulators have not historically
recognised Open Source software as a charitable purpose. We hope that by seeking charity status, we will help pave the
way for charity regulators worldwide to recognise the criticality of Open Source infrastructure.

“This effort is critical to the future sustainability of Open Source. The unique challenges the Open Source
 ecosystem is facing need the sort of Open Source thinking the Software Stewardship Lab is building. Open Source
 has never been more important. It's imperative we give it a strong future.”

We can't do this research without funding. In fact, without funding, we would be in the ironic situation where we
couldn't sustainably develop the very technology required for the Open Source ecosystem to be more sustainable. That's
a Catch-22 with serious ramifications.

We have seen that companies are willing to fund keystone Open Source projects, which is important.

But we're asking organisations to also fund Open Source sustainability research, simply because it acts as a force
multiplier — it creates tools that strengthen the entire ecosystem, not just individual projects. Each dollar funds
structural improvements to the foundations of our technological infrastructure.

We have various sponsorship arrangements available:

All our income and expenses will be detailed on Open Collective with full transparency.

Know that, if you are able to help fund our work, you are making a positive difference to the Open Source ecosystem that
the entire world relies on.

Open Source lies at the foundation of our modern technology. That technology can, and does, fall apart when keystone
projects are underfunded and insecure, and when maintainers are overworked. Existing solutions aren't doing enough to
preserve our critical infrastructure.

We can solve this problem together with your support. If you're able to, sponsor us.

title: EA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?
description:
The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
As if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. fullText:
The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun

As if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. EA Sports FC 27 (the franchise that used to be Fifa – what better time to no longer be Fifa-branded?) is due to be released on 25 September. I just spent two intense days in Vancouver, where the EA FC games are made, playing FC 27 and talking to its developers.

With an annual franchise such as EA FC, it helps to have something fresh to entice regular fans, and FC 27 has a whole new element, entitled the Grounds. It’s a physical hub-type area, similar to the City as seen in 2K’s recent NBA 2K basketball games, but much more pleasant to frequent, split as it is into areas inspired by British, French and Argentinian street-football culture.

The Grounds provides a new physical home for an existing element of EA FC: Clubs, its casual online mode in which you control a single player and play matches closer to kickabouts than real-world football, but beyond that, it has plenty of other activities and distractions.

I spent about an hour in the Grounds, and found it more enjoyable than expected. Among its buildings are playing areas, whose entrances act as lobbies where you can choose to play against random people or to set up a custom game with your FC 27-owning friends. Each playing area hosts a specific type of game, and the Grounds has a map that you can teleport around.

It rewards exploration: I encountered targets that could be smashed by spawning a football and drop-kicking it, some of which were clumped into mini-games. Its games offered clever twists on the Clubs blueprint. In one 3v3 game, target areas appeared for short periods, and if I scored from one, I got a bonus goal for my side. And one game based on dodgeball gave its players three lives, which they would lose if others successfully kicked a ball at them.

The Grounds should prove popular: it has been tastefully and cleverly constructed and will no doubt expand as new game-types are added. You could also envisage it, in future years, hosting a narrative mode along the line of the Journey from Fifa 17 to 19.

FC 26 marked a mission by EA Sports to improve the franchise’s responsiveness by enacting a surprising number of changes to its fundamental gameplay, and that process continues apace in FC 27.

Although anyone who played FC 26 will testify that those efforts actually caused some new problems, such as an annoying tendency for defensive interceptions to bounce back weirdly into the path of forwards. EA Sports, according to gameplay design director Kantcho Doskov, took radical action to eliminate such aberrations: “We had to completely strip out the existing system for interceptions and build a new one from scratch. We spent six months doing that.”

Via a build that let me play Champions League games between a limited number of teams, I found that to be a worthwhile exercise: those defensive bounce-backs were blissfully absent. But an awful lot more was also in evidence in FC 27 on the gameplay revamp front.

Much of this – perhaps counterintuitively at a time when AI is worming its way ever deeper into all our lives – involved paring back the in-game AI. That’s certainly the case for the defensive AI: whereas previously, defenders would rush towards the ball, getting pulled out of position and opening up annoying gaps, FC 27 now gives much more manual control over defensive jockeying, movement and tackles.

Crossing, previously AI-assisted, has been revamped in FC 27, leaving it up to me to get the direction and weight of cross right, then giving me more of a chance to position my centre-forward correctly. The AI controlling forward players, meanwhile, has been improved, so that off-the-ball players now move much more helpfully, allowing pass-and-move sequences, and they are much better at staying onside.

I was also impressed by revamped two-stage corner and free-kick systems. But FC 27, gameplay-wise, achieves what FC 26 set out to, this time with no evident anomalies, and feels more responsive to your inputs than any of its predecessors.

FC 27’s Career Mode, in which you get to play out your fantasies of managing your favourite team, has also been extensively revamped – primarily with a view towards making its transfer system more like the one that operates in the real world, and to force you to do more actual management.

The headline means of doing the latter is called Dynamic OVR. OVR is simply jargon for any player’s all-important overall rating; where previously OVRs remained constant, in FC 27’s Career Mode they will go up and down depending on form, fitness and general happiness. Thus, you will have to rest your best players over the course of a long season, but you may also be able to buy players cheaply with artificially low OVRs if, say, they are coming back from injury.

Pete O’Donnell, FC 27’s Career Mode game director, explains how the game’s transfer system has been modernised: “Previously, you could do things instantly, which was good for a game but was not very realistic. We looked at how clubs interact with each other, how they do the deals themselves, and we spoke to scouts and directors of football. Then it was about extracting the fun bits of those jobs.”

The new system will back you up with more data; now each player will have an xTV (Expected Transfer Value) rating, which should speed negotiations. FC 27 will also reflect clubs’ real-life transfer policies, according to O’Donnell, with clubs’ boards requesting that you sign certain players. Press conferences in FC 27 will force you to make decisions that will please some players and annoy others, and 20 Unexpected Events have been added to Career Mode.

FC 27’s Ultimate Transfer (FUT) mode, the hardcore card-based system that provides a home for most of FC’s loot box action, will have a new headline feature in the form of a Gallery, which will showcase all the players and card-sets collected, rather than just first 11s.

EA Sports says it has also “streamlined” FUT’s previously impenetrable Squad-Based Challenges (SBC) system, and has made a tweak designed to avert stalemates, which affected the latter stages in FUT in FC 26, by restricting plus-level FUT players to three, rather than five, play-styles. But the nature of FUT – which develops over a long period post-launch – means that it will take a while to ascertain whether those changes prove effective.

There will be another major change to FC 27 that has nothing to do with how it plays: because it contains microtransactions, it will now be rated 16+ rather than the previous 3+, after a policy change at age-rating organisation Pegi. Given the game’s enthusiastic young and teenage audience, we asked EA Sports’ top brass to comment, but they blandly responded: “While the game functionally remains the same, this has resulted in a new Pegi age rating. It marks a change in the way we are giving the information to players and parents.”

Beyond Pegi’s European jurisdiction, the game will be rated E for Everybody. But in the UK, parents should think hard about letting youngsters play a 16-rated game. If they are worried about their offspring racking up huge bills for FUT transactions, the good news is that a new Ultimate Plus Edition of the game, which includes loads of stuff that would previously have cost in-game currency, will go on sale. But the bad news is it costs £139.99 and will only be available as a pre-order before 31 August.

title: BBC NI to remain home of Irish Premiership coverage
description: BBC Sport NI agrees a new three-year broadcast deal with the Irish FA and Northern Ireland Football League to ensure the continuation of extensive free-to-air coverage of international and domestic football across BBC iPlayer, online, radio and TV.
fullText:
BBC Sport NI has agreed a new three-year broadcast deal with the Irish FA and Northern Ireland Football League to ensure the continuation of extensive free-to-air coverage of international and domestic football across BBC iPlayer, online, radio and TV.

The new deal means BBC Sport NI will show 30 live Boyle Sports Premiership streams per season - starting with Friday night's north Belfast derby between Cliftonville and Crusaders - as well as 10 senior Women's Northern Ireland international matches and action from domestic cup competitions.

Finals of the Clearer Water Irish Cup and BetMcLean Cup will be shown live on BBC television and BBC iPlayer, as well as streamed coverage of games in the former competition from the fifth round onwards.

Live coverage of the Irish Premiership will also continue on BBC Radio Ulster and BBC Sounds, while highlights from NIFL and Irish Cup games will be available across BBC platforms.

This follows confirmation that BBC Sport NI will broadcast every Northern Ireland senior men's international until June 2028.

"This new agreement strengthens our longstanding commitment to bringing audiences the very best coverage of the game in Northern Ireland, from national teams to domestic league and cup competitions," said Neil Brittain, the executive editor of BBC Sport NI.

"Through BBC iPlayer, digital platforms, television, radio and BBC Sounds, we will continue to make local football available to the widest possible audience."

Steven Mills, NIFL Chief Operations Officer, said: "We are delighted to extend our contract with BBC Sport NI and sincerely thank them for their continued commitment and significant investment in our game.

"Their coverage has played a major role in raising the profile of the Premiership, increasing its reach and supporting the continued growth of the league."

Colin McKendry, Irish Football Association President said: "We are delighted that the Clearer Water Irish Cup, our flagship domestic cup competition, and Northern Ireland senior women's international matches will continue to be showcased on BBC Sport NI.

"Their coverage has played a significant role in raising their profile reaching new audiences and inspiring more people to engage with football across Northern Ireland.

"Alongside them and our partners at NIFL, this agreement will ensure supporters have even more opportunities to watch, follow and enjoy the game, while helping to grow the sport at every level."

title: Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze
description: England international Lucy Bronze says a Uefa boycott of Fifa competitions would be the "right thing" for the future of the game.
fullText:
England defender Lucy Bronze says a Uefa boycott of Fifa competitions would be the "right thing" for the future of the game, despite the impact it could have on women's football.

After Fifa president Gianni Infantino announced a plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors, European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the proposals were dropped.

The plans have since been aborted - with Infantino apologising for his "errors" - but in a statement on Thursday, Uefa said the boycott could still go ahead.

Women's football would be the first to be impacted if Uefa's stance is upheld, with the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup due to start on 5 September.

Six European teams - England, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain and hosts Poland - are scheduled to play in the tournament.

"I think the players who play in those competitions, the European players, we stand by our beliefs and what the right thing is for our game," said Bronze, who was speaking in New Zealand on Chelsea's pre-season tour.

Mexico break ranks to join Argentina in backing Infantino

Infantino sorry for errors but stays Fifa president

She added: "And if that means boycotting competitions, then that has to happen.

"It's for the future of the game and not just for me today and tomorrow.

"It's for all the little girls or little boys who come after us to make sure that they're in a good place when the game's moving forward in decades to come, not just tomorrow."

In October, England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland all have qualifiers for next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

Should they not feature in the play-offs because of Uefa's boycott, European teams - including defending champions Spain - would not be able to participate in the tournament, which starts in June.

Also in October, the Under-17 Women's World Cup is scheduled to take place in Morocco.

Speaking to BBC Sport last week, former England defender Anita Asante said: "The first casualties will be women's football tournaments.

"If this isn't resolved by the time of England's qualifiers, then the impact could be huge and it is already a busy schedule."

Baroness Campbell, former Football Association director of women's football, said it was "tragic" that women's football could be first to be affected.

The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino, while Wales, Albania and Croatia are among other individual associations to have turned their back on the 56-year-old.

title: Norrie saves match point in superb Montreal fightback
description: Britain's Cameron Norrie saves a match point as he produces a superb fightback to beat world number seven Alex de Minaur at the Canadian Open.
fullText:
Britain's Cameron Norrie saved a match point as he produced a superb fightback to beat world number seven Alex de Minaur at the Canadian Open.

Norrie was a set and 5-2 down against the Australian third seed before coming through 5-7 7-6 (7-5) 6-1 to reach the fourth round.

De Minaur, leading by a double-break, had a match point on his own serve in the second set but double-faulted.

He twice served for the match but, at 5-4 up, double-faulted again to put the set back on level terms.

World number 37 Norrie edged the tie-break and then ran away with the deciding set to complete victory in two hours and 52 minutes.

"It was a great match to win and to test my level, and I can take so much confidence from this one," the 30-year-old said.

"The level was so high the first two sets.

"From the beginning, [de Minaur] came out firing and I had to match it."

Norrie - who reached the Los Cabos semi-finals last week - will face France's Arthur Fils for a place in the quarter-finals.

De Minaur's exit means that fifth seed Ben Shelton is the only top-10 men's player remaining in Montreal.

World number one Jannik Sinner and third-ranked Novak Djokovic withdrew before the tournament began, while top seed Alexander Zverev lost his first match.

Sixth-ranked Daniil Medvedev, seventh seed Taylor Fritz and world number nine Flavio Cobolli also all lost in the second round.

title: Norway call on Infantino to resign but two countries back Fifa president
description: The Norwegian Football Federation calls for Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign after he attempted to sell off stakes in the World Cup.
fullText:
Norway have called on Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign following his aborted attempt to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, but Mexico and Argentina have voiced their support for the 56-year-old.

Norway have gone a step further than the football associations of England, Wales, Croatia and Albania, all of whom have withdrawn support for Infantino without explicitly calling for him to resign.

"He [Infantino] does not have the institutional trust required to govern Fifa stably in the times we are in," Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness said on Friday.

"There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football cooperation is very much in trouble, and we must have a reason to get together now, and we want to ask the Fifa president to resign now.

"We will see which other countries eventually join in, if that becomes the strategy from the Uefa board. We are not going to ask for an extraordinary [Uefa board] meeting, we will ask him to resign in our dialogue with Fifa."

Klaveness, who is a qualified lawyer, went through a list of concerns that the Norwegian FA has expressed to Fifa during her four-year tenure.

Among them were questions around the awarding of tournaments, the inaugural Fifa peace prize that was awarded to US President ​Donald Trump in December, and the overturning of a ban for American forward Folarin Balogun during the recent World Cup following a phone call from Trump.

Fifa has been approached for comment.

Meanwhile, earlier on Friday the Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

Concacaf, which runs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, called for a "comprehensive reckoning" of Infantino's presidency after he aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

However, 2026 World Cup co-hosts Mexico have backed Infantino's leadership amid widespread calls for him to resign.

"The FMF [Mexican FA] supports president Infantino's leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening," a statement read.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa members.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

However, Conmebol did "express its concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue or the institutional mechanisms provided for dealing with this type of situation".

Meanwhile, the football association of 2026 World Cup runners-up Argentina praised Infantino for recognising and apologising for his "errors".

It described his decade-long tenure as Fifa president as "centred on the development of soccer worldwide and institutional strength based on a clear, stable, and transparent governance model".

Infantino is unanimously backed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), but faces opposition from European football's governing Uefa and Concacaf.

European teams could still boycott the World Cup as Uefa said its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted.

Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".

The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino, while Wales, Albania and Croatia are among other individual associations to have turned their back on the 56-year-old.

Concacaf described Infantino's proposal as "a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first", and that "this recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour".

However, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president.

Before Infantino withdrew his proposal, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood "in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf in opposition to the plans.

Ordinarily, Infantino would not be able to stand for re-election in March.

The maximum tenure under Fifa statutes is three four-year terms, and Infantino is hoping to be voted in for a fourth time.

However, after replacing Sepp Blatter in 2016, his first term lasted only three years. He successfully argued this one should not count, which allows him to stand again.

Infantino was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 unopposed, and before the FFE controversy it looked certain the same would apply in 2027.

Now Uefa and Infantino's other opponents must try to find a candidate to stand against him.

The deadline for names to be put forward, together with at least five letters of support from member associations, is 18 November.

The election, by secret ballot, will then take place at the 77th Fifa Congress in Rabat, Morocco on 18 March.

If two candidates stand for election, a simple majority of the 211 member associations is required to win.

If there are three or more candidates, 75% of votes is required to win outright. If that threshold is not met, the candidate with the fewest votes is removed and another vote is held.

Once the field is reduced to two candidates, it becomes a simple majority.

Unless Uefa can find a way to unseat Infantino, he has seven months to cement his supporter base.

One way Infantino has always done this is by jetting off around the world and meeting people.

When he was elected in 2016, Infantino declared that Uefa gave him a budget of €500,000 (£430,000), external "to fund flights - mainly flights - around the world" to lobby member associations for votes.

Following Wednesday's meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Infantino jetted off to South America for the inauguration of new Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Another key tool will be the funding of the 211 member associations, which has enabled Infantino to build loyalty around the world.

This is especially true among developing nations who cannot afford to pay for football development.

Crucially, the latest iteration of Infantino's investment programme, Fifa Forward 3.0, ends in December. It has given all national associations up to $8m (£5.94m) in the latest four-year cycle, a 30% increase on the last one.

When announced, Fifa Forward 4.0 may well up the level of funding again.

For this reason, outside of Europe, Infantino still has a great deal of support and would be the favourite to win an election.

Infantino's staunchest critics, though a few could break the block vote against him.

The African confederation has reaffirmed its unanimous support for Infantino.

While the Asian confederation joined Uefa in criticising FFE it did not issue any statement after the plan was aborted. So far, only Jordan - who did not support Infantino anyway - has said it will not vote for him.

Has strongly criticised Infantino, but Mexico has already broken away to back the president. With so many small nations in the region which benefit from Infantino's funding, it is unknown how much of the rest of the block will hold.

The OFC will not offer a statement until it holds a meeting next month, but earlier this year president Lambert Maltock called Infantino a "leader par excellence" and lauded his investment in grassroots.

A statement issued on Thursday amounted to "do it again and we won't vote for you", but Infantino can still count on Conmebol. Argentina and Paraguay are among the countries to publicly back his re-election.

title: England forward Toney charged with assault
description: Ivan Toney, who was part of England's World Cup squad this summer, is charged with assault following an incident last December.
fullText:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

fullText:
Researchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questions

Scientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe.

The viruses are specific kinds known as bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria and are used around the world to treat patients with persistent infections. In lab tests, a cocktail of the AI-designed viruses killed E coli bugs that were resistant to natural bacteriophages.

Dr Brian Hie, a chemical engineer at Stanford University in California, used genome language models, the genetic equivalent of the large language models behind AI chatbots, to design functioning genomes for bacteriophages. The viruses were then made in the laboratory and pitted against E coli in a dish.

The ability to “rapidly design” genomes and tune them for specific bugs while overcoming resistance could “transform phage therapy” and “expand biotechnological toolkits”, the researchers wrote in the journal Science.

But beyond the potential benefits, the scientists said the work raised “important biosafety, biocontainment and biosecurity considerations” and urged others who were designing whole genomes to “consult both safety and security professionals throughout the project”.

In an accompanying article, Prof Tom Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke at the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, reinforced the warning, writing: “Although this is promising for life sciences applications, it also raises urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions. The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.”

Hie and his colleagues used AI models called Evo1 and Evo2 to design the new viral genomes. The models were trained on genetic data from 2 million bacteriophages. The genetic code for viruses that can infect plants, humans or other animals was intentionally excluded from the AI’s training to reduce the risk of it designing dangerous viruses.

The AI generated thousands of potential genomes from which the researchers selected nearly 300 to make in the lab. These were dropped into bacteria, which read the genetic code and churned out the new bacteriophages. The process was not efficient: only 16 bacteriophages proved to be viable, but a cocktail of them swiftly overcame resistance in two different strains of E coli.

Bacteriophage genomes are tiny, but Inglesby and Hanke said the work nevertheless proved that generative AI could create functioning viral genomes. Whether the same approach could be applied to other viruses was unknown, but they said work on pathogens that could infect humans, animals or plants should not be pursued.

“Such genomes might encode new pathogens that … cannot be contained by existing countermeasures,” they wrote.

Tom Ellis, a professor of synthetic genome engineering at Imperial College London, said the work was impressive, but revealed how hard it would be to make more complex genomes. “This is literally the smallest and easiest genome to make,” he said.

An AI trained on the genetic code of dangerous bugs could be used to design more harmful viruses, Ellis said, but controlling access to genetic data and having restrictions on making genomes that look dangerous would help. “Governments are working hard to do this already,” he added.

“But honestly,” he said, “the threat from full AI design and writing of a genome of a virus or bacteria is very overblown when we consider that just taking existing pathogens and making gain-of-function changes to their genomes is so much easier and much more likely to be a real pathogenic threat.”

Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London, said the most important point to intervene at the moment was when DNA was being manufactured. “It’s important to see the bigger governance picture and not focus regulation solely on the AI model,” she said. “A layered approach makes more sense: safeguards around model development and access, responsible research review, synthesis screening, and established laboratory biosafety and biosecurity.”

title: One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about a AI. Does he also hold the remedy? | Alan Finkel
description:

Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk predicted in July that legions of AI-powered robots would dominate the physical world and that AI might not take orders from people any more.
